entries.topicDescription: Persistent storage and object-graph management on Apple platforms.

tips.title: SwiftData uses macros for zero-boilerplate models
tips.content:
SwiftData (iOS 17+) replaces Core Data's verbose setup with
a single @Model macro. Annotate your class and you get
persistence, change tracking, and undo support automatically.

Properties are persisted by default. Use @Transient for
computed or non-persistent properties. Relationships are
inferred from type annotations.

The @Model macro generates the schema, migration plan, and
property wrappers behind the scenes. No .xcdatamodeld files,
no NSManagedObject subclasses, no code generation steps.

SwiftData integrates natively with SwiftUI through @Query
and the modelContainer modifier, making data flow seamless.

tips.title: Predicates and sort descriptors filter efficiently
tips.content:
Both Core Data and SwiftData support predicates for filtering
data at the database level. This is much faster than fetching
everything and filtering in memory.

SwiftData uses the #Predicate macro with Swift's native syntax.
No more stringly-typed NSPredicate format strings — you get
compile-time checking and autocompletion.

Sort descriptors determine the order of results. Chain multiple
sort descriptors for hierarchical sorting (sort by category,
then by date within each category).

Use @Query in SwiftUI views to declare your fetch request
declaratively. The view re-renders automatically when
matching data changes.

tips.title: Model containers and contexts manage the persistence stack
tips.content:
In SwiftData, the ModelContainer holds the schema and storage
configuration. The ModelContext is your workspace for creating,
reading, updating, and deleting model objects.

Set up the container once at the app level using the
.modelContainer modifier. SwiftUI automatically provides a
context to all child views via the environment.

For background work, create a separate ModelContext from the
container. Each context is isolated — changes aren't visible
to other contexts until you save.

Always save explicitly when doing batch operations. SwiftUI's
auto-save handles most cases, but background contexts need
manual context.save() calls.
